name: Tocantins
summary_text: Tocantins has no LGBTI statute of its own in this inventory; the state stands entirely under Brazil's national framework, which applies identically in Palmas and in any other Brazilian jurisdiction. Same-sex marriage has been legal nationwide since the National Council of Justice Resolution of 14 May 2013, adopted 14–1, and joint adoption has been available since 2010 with full equal rights from 2015.  Name and gender-marker change at the civil registry has required no surgery, hormones or diagnosis since the Supreme Federal Court ruling of 1 March 2018 and proceeds on self-determination. Brazil has no third-gender option nationwide, but civil-registry entries marked non-binary or unspecified have been possible since 2020, and a Superior Court of Justice ruling of 6 May 2025 permits rectification of registry entries to a neutral gender as precedent.  On 13 June 2019 the Supreme Federal Court held, in ADO 26 and MI 4733, that discrimination and violence on grounds of sexual orientation or gender identity constitutes a crime equivalent to racism under Law 7.716/1989, punishable by imprisonment of one to five years and fines. The April 2026 law-firm guide confirms that homophobia and transphobia are covered on the same footing, and that these national provisions, not any Tocantins statute, supply the criminal protection a trans visitor would rely on.  Entry and family matters follow the national rules: an expatriate legal guide updated in April 2026 records that same-sex marriage, spousal-visa equality and gender-marker rules operate nationwide, so a visitor's status and documents are handled on the same footing as anyone else's at the border.  The protective text does not describe routine experience. OutRight International's report of 12 March 2026 states that Brazil retains one of the world's highest rates of violence against sexual and gender minorities, particularly trans people, while its legal advances face repeal pressure in a conservative Congress. The April 2026 law-firm guide records that enforcement is uneven in practice, contrasting major urban centres, broadly welcoming and served by established legal infrastructure, against smaller cities and rural areas, where identical legal rights may still meet more social friction.

name: Alberta
summary_text: Alberta is a province of Canada and stands under the national framework. Gender identity and gender expression are protected grounds under the Canadian Human Rights Act and under the hate-motivation provisions of the Criminal Code, both added by Bill C-16, which the Senate passed 67-11 in June 2017, and courts have applied those protections consistently. No Canadian jurisdiction restricts trans people's use of restrooms or other sex-segregated facilities, entry carries no trans-specific friction, and identity documents issued federally can carry an X marker. Canadian authorities have issued no alert specific to trans travellers.  Alberta's own legislation runs against that framework. A package of three measures affecting transgender people as a class passed its final legislative stage on 4 December 2024: the Education Amendment Act 2024, which requires parental opt-in for classroom instruction and sets rules on student pronouns and sport; a health-statutes act barring certain gender-affirming care for minors; and a sports policy restricting trans participation. Premier Danielle Smith announced the package on 12 February 2024. Egale Canada and the Skipping Stone Foundation announced constitutional litigation on the day of passage, calling the measures discriminatory.  The laws are in force and shielded from challenge. Bill 9, the Protecting Alberta's Children Statutes Amendment Act, passed at the tail of the fall sitting and invokes the Charter's notwithstanding clause to insulate the three measures from legal challenge for years. Egale Canada, the Skipping Stone Foundation and five families say their court challenge to the underlying education act continues regardless, so the constitutional outcome remains unresolved while the statutes operate.  The package was scoped to exclude detention and certain facilities. The February 2024 announcement stated that the bans would not include women's shelters, women's prisons or public changing rooms, and no provincial rule placing trans prisoners by birth sex was enacted. For an adult trans visitor, the practical provincial exposure is therefore concentrated in schools, organised sport and access to gender-affirming care for minors accompanying them, rather than in custody or everyday facilities.  Custody inside Alberta runs on federal policy. Since 2018 the Correctional Service of Canada has accommodated offenders by gender identity rather than sex assigned at birth, and permits gender-diverse offenders to request placement or transfer to a men's or women's institution aligned with their gender identity or expression, regardless of anatomy or the sex or gender marker on identity documents; a request is refused only where the service finds unresolvable overriding health or safety concerns. As of 2025 the service reported 90 self-identified transgender women in federal institutions, 73 housed in men's institutions and 17 in women's. After Bill C-16, federal policy is that transgender prisoners are to be placed according to their gender identity, and prisoners held for more than 12 continuous months are to be considered for sex-reassignment surgery.  Correctional conditions remain the weakest point in the record. Lawyer Barbara findlay represented the transgender prisoner Synthia Kavanagh in litigation over gender-affirming medical treatment and placement in a women's institution. The Office of the Correctional Investigator called the 2022 gender-diversity policy an important change but flagged the absence of clear parameters for what counts as an overriding health or safety concern and the absence of a dedicated mechanism for gender-diverse prisoners to report abuse. A 2022 report alleged a pattern of abuse and discrimination against gender-diverse prisoners in Canadian jails and a higher likelihood of sexual assault; a 2022 study of Nova Scotia correctional officers found them generally mindful of trans-prisoner safety and security, with some concerns about risk to other prisoners. These concerns reach a trans visitor only if the visitor is detained.

sources.title: Vriend v Alberta - Supreme Court of Canada (1998)
sources.documents: Found Alberta legislature's failure to include sexual orientation as prohibited ground in provincial human rights law was itself a violation of Section 15 Charter rights; foundation for later explicit protection of sexual orientation and gender identity.
sources.detail: Cited as 'its 1998 decision in Vriend v Alberta' under Constitutional framework / Legal and equality rights; no URL visible in excerpt
